questions.q: What is the main drawback of manual scripted deployment as release frequency and environment count grow?
options: It becomes error-prone and slow — it's easy to run scripts out of order or skip one in a given environment
It requires a DACPAC to work at all
SQL Server disables manual scripts above a certain database size
It cannot be reviewed by a human before running
questions.explain: Manual scripting scales poorly: missed or out-of-order scripts across environments is exactly how schema drift starts.

questions.q: How does DACPAC-based deployment decide what change script to run?
options: A tool compares the compiled DACPAC against the live target database and generates the diff script automatically
It requires the DBA to hand-write every ALTER statement
It randomly selects changes from source control
It always drops and recreates the entire database
questions.explain: sqlpackage.exe (or SSDT's publish action) diffs the DACPAC against the live database's actual current state and generates the change script.

questions.q: What is a key tradeoff of DACPAC-based deployment mentioned in this lesson?
options: It's schema-only — data migrations like backfilling a column still need to be scripted and coordinated separately
It cannot be used with SSDT database projects
It only works on Azure SQL Database, never on-premises
It requires disabling all constraints before running
questions.explain: DACPACs handle schema (tables, views, procedures) but aren't designed to carry data migration logic.

questions.q: How do migration-based tools (the category Flyway, Liquibase, and DbUp represent) track deployment differently from a DACPAC?
options: They run numbered, one-directional migration scripts in order, tracked in a table, rather than diffing current state against intended state
They require no tracking at all
They only support Oracle databases
They automatically generate rollback scripts with no extra work
questions.explain: Migration tools take a version-based approach: each change is a numbered script, and a tracking table records which have already run.

questions.q: What problem does the expand-contract pattern solve?
options: Making a schema change to a live, actively-used table without downtime, by staging the change across expand, migrate, and contract steps
Compressing a database file to save disk space
Automatically resolving schema drift between environments
Encrypting sensitive columns during deployment
questions.explain: Expand-contract adds the new structure first, migrates usage over, and only removes the old structure once nothing depends on it — avoiding a single breaking instant change.
